title: SYSK Selects: How Cult Deprogramming Works
summary: SYSK Selects rerun (originally from September 2015) on cult deprogramming. Hosts trace the early-1970s rise of "cults" (many Bible-based or Eastern-influenced new religious movements) and the parental and anti-cult reaction that led to forcible deprogramming. They cover Ted Patrick and the Cult Awareness Network, the legal loophole of conservatorship, the Stephanie Ryth Miller case in Ohio, the Jason Scott case that bankrupted CAN and ended with Scientology buying its assets, Rick Ross and modern exit counseling, and the ethical muddle around the practice. The episode closes with listener mail about a hot air balloon landing near the San Francisco Bay.

segments.title: Rerun intro and opening banter
segments.summary: Chuck introduces this Saturday Select rerun from September 2015 about cult deprogramming. Hosts banter about cults, brainwashing, and the show's premise.

segments.title: 1970s cults and generational divide
segments.summary: Hosts describe the late-1960s and 1970s generational rift and the rise of groups then called cults, mostly Bible-based Christian groups and Eastern-influenced movements, now often called new religious movements. The Jonestown tragedy and the Manson family made people see cults as dangerous.

segments.title: Ted Patrick and the Cult Awareness Network
segments.summary: Ted Patrick, a high school dropout, began deprogramming after a job infiltrating the Children of God, and later led the Cult Awareness Network. Parents paid up to around a thousand dollars per case. The hosts explain the legal theory that parents could consent to kidnapping their minors.

segments.title: Conservatorship loophole and legal protection
segments.summary: Adult cult members could be placed under conservatorship based on loose proof of mental illness, with psychologists testifying that cult membership itself showed mental illness. Courts and public opinion, fueled by fears of a communist or mind-control conspiracy, often sided with deprogrammers.

segments.title: Patrick's methods and notable victims
segments.summary: Patrick initially hired street thugs for abductions and later worked with Sandra Sachs and a henchman called Goose. Victims included people who were not in cults, such as a woman who left the Greek Orthodox Church and an English professor and activist. The hosts describe how deprogramming involved sleep and food deprivation, constant berating, and a reported snapping or conversion back that was cited as proof it worked.

segments.title: Stephanie Ryth Miller case
segments.summary: Stephanie Ryth Miller, a nineteen-year-old lesbian, was abducted in Ohio by Patrick's crew after her parents paid around eight thousand dollars, then was taken to Alabama and raped over seven days in an attempt to change her sexuality. The trial judge, Simon Lesh, reportedly said the parents acted out of love and the case ended without punishment for the parents.

segments.title: Jason Scott case and Scientology takeover of CAN
segments.summary: Jason Scott was held in Washington State by deprogrammers Mark Workman and Charles Simpson after leaving a Pentecostal church, and escaped by faking a change of belief. A civil suit backed by Scientology lawyers bankrupted the Cult Awareness Network, which Scientology then bought and renamed. Scott later settled for a small amount plus Rick Ross's services.

segments.title: Exit counseling and the moral muddle
segments.summary: Rick Ross now runs exit counseling, a voluntary family-based intervention, in contrast to coercive deprogramming. The hosts discuss the moral ambiguity, since some former members say deprogramming helped them, and the danger of lumping all new religions under the word cult. They mention Ted Patrick's book Let Our Children Go and a possible future episode on the Satanic panic.

segments.title: Listener mail: hot air balloon landing
segments.summary: Listener Ryan from Washington, D.C., who worked on a Napa Valley hot air balloon crew, describes an emergency landing in a wheat field near San Francisco Bay and paying the landowner with champagne.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts thank listeners, give social and email contacts, and close the show.
